title: Faster AI Responses with Semantic Caching in Azure Managed Redis | OD823

segments.text: SHRUTI PATHAK: Hello, everyone.
My name is Shruti.
I'm a Product Manager for Azure Managed Redis.
And today, we'll talk about how Azure Managed Redis is the new
age Redis, Managed Redis on Azure, and how it helps
with building AI apps at the internet scale.
So most of you must be familiar with Redis.
It has been around for a long time.
You are probably using it already for your session store,
for leaderboard, for reducing database cost,
or making your databases more performant.
Redis use cases have recently expanded along
with the internet scale.
It started out with some basic traditional scenarios,
but Redis now has many more use cases that it can support,
like time series, vector searches,
JSON data, semantic caching.
Times have changed.
The internet scale has changed,
and so has the Redis use cases have expanded as well.
So today, we'll be quickly covering what's new with Redis,
especially the Azure Managed Redis.
Azure Managed Redis is a fully managed in-memory data store
on Azure.
It's a first-party offering on Azure, and it's based
on the Redis Enterprise software,
which offers a much more cost-effective TCO compared
to the Azure Cache for Redis offering.
And it's also much more performant.
It's up to 15% more -- 15 times, sorry, not 15% --
15 times much more performant
than the Azure Cache for Redis offerings.
It is zone redundant by default.
It has four nines offering by default, and obviously,
you can also set it up with a five 9s setup
with a geo-replication,
which will give you the five 9s of availability SLA.
As with the Redis software,
it can support your accelerations scenarios
for your applications.
You can use Redis as a distributed cache.
You can use it for session management.
You can use it for leaderboards, pub/sub.
You name it.
There's so many scenarios where you can use Redis.
But alongside those, Azure Managed Redis is also able
to power your RAG scenarios, and you can also use it
as a lightweight vector data store as well.
How is that possible?
So we'll talk about the secret source a little bit.
How does Azure Managed Redis do that?
But first, let's look at the state of AI agents today.
So AI agents today -- this is a very simple depiction,
but there's an input that usually a user provides,
or there's some triggers or events
that trigger the AI agent.
And internally, the AI agent is essentially a bunch
of instructions, a model, and a lot of tool calls
that enrich what the agent can do.
And then obviously, it produces some kind of output
that makes it more -- that makes it productive.
But if you look at the tool calls that the agent needs
to enrich itself, it needs knowledge that's specific
to your domain.
It needs to be able to execute some actions
so that it's more impactful, and then obviously,
it needs memory as well.
So these are -- this is a high-level overview
of what actually an agent looks like.
But if you start doing agents in production,
lot of challenges start coming up.
Gartner predicts that 40%
of enterprise applications will have specific AI agents
by the year 2026.
So this is already up from 2025, where 2025 didn't have a lot
of AI-specific -- task-specific agents,
and that number is growing up this year,
and it will continue next year as well.
But once you start putting AI agents in production,
there's some challenges that are going to show up.
The pace of innovation in the AI world is tremendous.
How do you keep up with the pace?
How do you keep yourself abreast with the new innovations,
the new things that are happening in vector search?
How do you use or how do you adopt those things
for your production scenarios?
So that's one challenge.
The other one is unpredictable cost.
A lot of this is new for most of us, the way tokens work,
the way token score relate to the dollar amount
that you end up paying.
A lot of times, you will see -- you get surprises at the end
of the month when you see your bill.
So there's unpredictable cost in there.
Model calls are expensive, and they take a lot of time as well.
So there's this cost aspect as well that's quite challenging.
And these agents, as we just saw in the previous screen,
agents need context, and agents need memory
to be more impactful.
Once you solve all of these challenges,
that's when you will be able to build enterprise-ready,
internet-scale AI agents.
So today, we'll be mostly covering these two challenges:
the cost management and context and memory.
How do you solve these two challenges
with Azure Managed Redis?
So I have my friends Phil and Roy,
who will join a little bit later, who will talk
about these challenges one by one.
So how does Azure Managed Redis do that?
So the secret sauce is the Redis search module that comes in,
that you can configure at no extra cost.
So the Redis search module allows Azure Managed Redis
to do vector similarity search on embeddings
that you store inside of Redis.
So once you configure this module, it allows you
to do a similarity search on vectors,
and that powers both the cost savings and the context --
the memory context scenarios that I just mentioned.
Now that I've given up the secret sauce, I think it's time
for me to take a backseat and let Phil and Roy later
on show you all the magic and how it happens.
So this was it from my side.
Take it over, Phil.
PHILIP LAUSSERMAIR: Hi, everyone.
My name is Philip Laussermair.
I'm a Senior Solutions Architect at Redis, and I specialize
in Azure Managed Redis.
As Shruti mentioned, I'm really excited to walk you through one
of our top AI use cases, semantic caching,
and it's all powered
by our semantic search capability in Redis Search.
So if you know Redis, you probably think of caching.
This is one of our bread-and-butter use cases.
This is what we actually were founded on.
And for the last 10 years or so,
this is really what we focused on.
And the typical pattern, you see it here.
You put it in front of a database.
It's meant to offload a lot of repetitive costs,
take off pressure from the database, improve performance.
And that's the typical pattern.
You check the cache,
if the existing key is already in there.
If it is, you serve it to the customer.
If not, you call the database and then load it back
into your Redis instance.
So this works extremely well.
In any best practice with databases,
you'll probably see caching come up as one of the first ways
to optimize and improve.
But a lot of things, as Shruti has mentioned,
has changed in the last decade or so, especially in the last,
let's say, two or three years
with the advent of generative AI.
So, at Redis, what we've been able
to do is exact key-value match caching is not ideal for LLMs.
I could ask a query that Shruti could send
in a few minutes later in a slightly different variation,
but it could be the same underlying intent.
It could have the same meaning.
And in that scenario, tokens are expensive.
You're going to generate a full amount of tokens for a scenario
where you potentially could have saved on that.
And that's where semantic caching comes into play.
So the general idea stays the same.
We're going to check Redis, see if there's a cache hit.
If not, instead of calling a database,
we're going to call an LLM.
But really how this is all being powered is now you can store
your vector embeddings in your Redis instance,
and then using vector similarity search, as prompts come in,
we can then check the cache, compare the similarity,
and based on a threshold that you would set, that determines
if it was similar enough to be a cache hit or not.
And we actually have a demo,
so I can show you this live what this would look like,
how it would be for you or your customers.
But at the end of the day, the idea is this is really meant
to save on tokens, which we all see
in the news day in and day out.
Token cost is exploding.
Response time, of course, is a huge performance factor.
The agents are running longer and longer.
They're getting much more intelligent, but that could lead
to seconds or even minutes of wait time.
And then finally, consistency.
There's certain use cases where you sometimes don't want an LLM
to be so non-deterministic.
If you're going to ask it the same prompt
or the same underlying intent every time, you want to be able
to have a sense of confidence
that you're promoting the same answer that you intend.
So it gives you some confidence from that angle as well.
But now that we have a general understanding
of the underlying architecture, why don't we jump into a demo,
and that should make it a lot more clear and pretty exciting.
Okay. So now we're in our semantic caching demo here.
So just to orient you, I want
to show you what you're looking at here.
On the left side, I want you to think of just a regular LLM,
take Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude.
That's the left side.
The right side is the same idea,
but with semantic caching underneath the hood,
powered by an Azure Managed Redis instance,
live as we go along.
I want to point out a few other items, some metrics down here
that will capture every time we send a prompt.
But really, without further ado, we can jump right in.
So let's say we were going to send a prompt,
"How do I improve product search relevance using
vector embeddings?"
Let's pretend we're an e-commerce company, Contoso,
and this might be a typical question that would be asked.
So what's happening right now is both are acting
like a typical LLM.
I sent a query.
We're going to get a response.
They were two separate responses.
So generative AI being non-deterministic.
You can see the same query
at relatively the same exact moment gave me similar
but a little different answers.
The one on the left took 118 tokens.
The one on the right, 131.
And both were roughly between one to two seconds in timing.
So now let's take a similarly phrased search,
but not exactly the same value.
So instead of "How do I improve product search relevance using
vector embeddings?"
let's just change it up,
"How can vector embeddings make product search more relevant?"
And what I want you to take a focus on is right on the right,
what you saw was a semantic cache hit.
So the first thing you notice was it was extremely fast.
The second thing you'll notice is it is the exact
same response.
So we're taking advantage of that previous response.
And so no tokens were generated.
That's one of the biggest things to highlight.
On the left here, since this was just our normal LLM call,
every time we send a request, we're going to get a response.
It did go and generate another 126 tokens.
As you can see, very similar, but for this kind of query,
we didn't get to take advantage of the previous one.
So every time, it's just going to make net new calls.
So I want to show you one other thing.
If I click here on this query, these are the steps
that actually happened underneath the hood
in that almost millisecond it took to get the response back.
So the first few things, first off, of course,
we're going to check the cache.
There's different ways you can optimize semantic caching.
The first one being we actually can do an exact cache lookup.
So if it was a key-value pair, we could take advantage of that
and actually just serve it like a data cache would.
Since that didn't exist, we then went
and generated our embeddings.
We got our embeddings back,
and did the vector similarity search.
Based on our threshold,
the cosine similarity was high enough
that it triggered a cache hit.
And so that's what you saw as the end user.
You got that result super fast, with no tokens being spent.
So just to show you what it would look like again
in the same scenario
with another query not related to any of these.
If I fire it off, both are going to act just
like typical LLMs, respond.
The reason I highlight that is this is all running every single
time underneath the hood.
Because Redis is an in-memory database, it's lightning fast.
So just because this is happening,
customers aren't sitting around waiting.
If I throw in more, you'll see it's just --
you wouldn't notice it was running any other time.
So next, I want to show some more deep dives
on vector similarity search.
So taking our first prompt, let's see,
"What's the most cost-effective caching strategy
for serving personalized product recommendations
to 10 million daily active users?"
Then we have a few variations below
that are either extremely similar or even unrelated.
So what I'm going to do is I'm just going to run a test
that is generating the similarity using a cosine vector
similarity search.
And this similarity threshold here is what you would set
in your application or client.
That's the threshold that you are comfortable
with for what would trigger a semantic cache hit or not.
So just here what we generated, at a 50% similarity threshold,
it would need to clear.
We can see that these top four prompts would be considered a
semantic cache hit.
If we wanted to increase that, let's say we wanted to go
to 75%, the first thing you notice is this variation four.
It's no longer considered similar enough
to do a semantic cache hit.
I should call out this first one, prompt cache hit.
This is that exact same key-value pair.
So this is going to be a match 100% of the time
because it's an exact key-value pair.
And finally, if we wanted to be super strict
and went all the way up to 90%, every single one
of these would be a miss.
So that gives you the flexibility
of how strict you want each scenario to be
with your threshold using vector similarity search.
Finally, I want to show you another scenario
of what it looks like for your end users that are being powered
by the same Managed Redis instance,
where you might be thinking, "Okay, this is great.
I love these semantic cache hits.
It saves a lot of tokens,
but how do I ensure no data leakage?"
If someone asks a very similar question,
but they have specific data to them that the LLM is using,
how do I make sure that's not being shown to anyone else?
So we have our two users here: Merchandiser Mia
and Platform Priya, and they have different roles in Contoso.
And what we're going to do is we're just going to ask,
based on some memory we have on the users, "What is your role?"
So on the left, Merchandiser Mia,
on the right, Platform Priya.
And I'm going to show you again, first, LLM call, nothing there.
Let's say, "What's my job?"
If I send that one, what you're going
to notice is each got a semantic cache hit, but strictly
on the keys we have saved for them.
And how that's being done is in the way you structure your keys
in Redis, you would actually set
up the naming convention specific to each user or domain
or whatever fits your use case,
and the search engine can be queried based
on that formula, essentially.
So in this example, we want to make sure that it's
in a per-user format so that there's no chance of leakage.
On the flip side, there are cases
where you actually want a global cache,
and that one would be something like an FAQ bot,
where it doesn't matter who the user is.
They're all going to be asking similar questions,
and you really want to take advantage of those.
So let's pretend this is our FAQ bot on our Contoso website
that unauthenticated users can come and use.
So let's start with the first one:
"What are just -- what are your hours?"
And these are semantically different.
This one was considered a cache hit
because it was similar enough to this.
This is just a vanilla LLM, so it doesn't have hours.
But you can start to see where, in these public instances,
you can generate a lot of semantic cache hits
and save a lot of tokens.
If this visitor B was a user that was coming in, say,
five minutes later,
they wouldn't know any different based on these responses,
obviously using real company data.
But in that scenario, almost every response
in this chain would be a semantic cache hit,
and there would be no tokens spent in that scenario.
So, again, one of the benefits and the flexibility
of either a global or per-user cache.
Finally, just to wrap up, I want to give you a sense
of what does this look like at scale.
So a quick calculator of what this looks
like in an enterprise use case.
Let's even drop this down to say 200,000 daily queries,
a 70% semantic cache hit rate, extremely low on the token sort
of budget in this scenario, and the pricing of GPT-5.
So, in this scenario, on an annualized basis,
that would be just
about $300,000 a year for your token spend.
And the way to think about the savings
with semantic caching is whatever your cache hit rate
percentage is, that is your net savings.
So with a 70% cache hit rate,
we're going to get 70% savings off of this overall spend.
And so what that comes out to is just
under 100,000, around 90,000 a year.
This also factors in both the embedding cost
that you would have to pay for for each query,
and the actual Redis instance
that could power a load like this.
And as you can see, even factoring those
in over an annualized basis, that would save over $200,000.
The last thing before I wrap up is I want to call
out this break-even rate.
This is the number of semantic cache hits that you would need
to have in your setup for this to be break-even.
So what this is saying, at a 1.2% cache hit rate,
you only need one out of 100 queries in your setup
to be a semantic cache hit for this
to ultimately save you any money net after that first query.
So, again, it's very scalable.
Once you set in place, you can kind of leave them there.
It really helps with performance.
It helps with token spend.
But overall, that is semantic caching
with Azure Managed Redis.
And now I am happy to pass it over to Roy,
who's going to talk a little bit
about how you can use Azure Managed Redis
for agent memory at the same time.
Thanks everyone.
ROY DE MILDE: Thank you, Phil.
And also, Shruti, thank you for the great presentation
and the demo and everything that we saw.
So I'm Roy, based out of the Netherlands.
I'm a Solutions Architect for Azure Managed Redis,
covering EMEA, and working with customers and partners
to make them successful
when they are adopting Azure Managed Redis.
I'm going to talk a little bit about agent memory.
I'm just going to explain why that is important
and how you can use AMR for that, and then I will jump
into a quick demo as well to showcase that.
So when we think about an agentic workflow
or an agentic AI system, we're thinking
about different agents working together to make sure
that you have highly fulfilling AI tasks.
But those agents can act even better when you're thinking
about when they can leverage memory as well.
The way we determine this is
that we have these short-term memory and the long-term memory.
So, for short-term memory, we often think
about the interaction, the conversation, a certain state,
and stuff like that, that we are saving
within that short-term memory capability.
But then, if you look at the long-term memory,
we think about from a personalization perspective.
When a user is interacting with the AI system,
you basically want the AI system to be aware.
What are the preferences?
What is some of the things that are important
for this specific user?
Or what is something of their interest and stuff like that?
And you can go nuts with this.
The world's your oyster if you think about it.
So what we are doing is splitting those two out,
more on the conversation history and state aspect,
and also the preferences, the behavior, the durable facts,
and the interest for a real personalization type
of interaction.
Now, when you think about this, and a user is interacting
with your systems, now the agents can have rapidly fast
access to that data.
And they can use that when they are determining they're using
specific tools, they're creating, they're using an LLM
to do certain reasoning about it, whatever you have built,
but they can rapidly fast get that data and include
that within the whole pattern that they are doing.
And this is where Azure Managed Redis really, really shines
if you are saving that specific data into AMR.
And also think about when agents are working together,
and a specific agent wants to give context to the other agent,
it's stored within AMR, so it can just easily say,
"Hey, have a look at this."
And now the new agent that needs to do something else
within the agentic workflow, they can grab that information
as well, giving you a way better experience as a user,
but also allowing you to interact better
with your consumers and your users.
So I do have a small demo around this.
So I'm going to hop over to another screen.
Just give me one sec real quick.
So here you can see the demo that we have built.
So basically, it's the same context of the previous demo
that you have seen by Phil.
So on the left-hand side,
you see the without memory capabilities,
and on the right-hand side,
you see the with memory capabilities.
So this is everything around personalization,
and that's how we have built this.
So this is basically an AI system where I can interact
with the system, and the system knows about me.
It has stored the conversations that we had,
and it has stored the durable facts, the preferences,
what type of work do I do.
So in this scenario, let me hop over to myself,
and let me just basically teach the AI a little bit about me.
So I'm going to say, "Hey, I'm a software engineer working
on machine learning projects, and I love hiking,
photography on the weekends."
So when I'm going to send that to both, you're going to see
on the left-hand side, it's going to respond like,
"Hey, nice to meet you.
Great." But nothing is being saved --
not on the conversational side,
not on the long-term memory side.
On the right-hand side, you actually see
that we are analyzing the message.
We can give a response back, and we're going
to remember certain facts about this user.
In this case, this is me.
So the user is a software engineer, and it loves hiking,
and it loves photography.
And if we actually look to the agent activity log,
it runs through a specific aspect of things to do
to analyze the message, reason about the message,
and also saving the aspects that we want to save
to the long-term memory.
So now, because we have stored the long-term memory facts
in effect to database as a hash vector,
I can also use semantic search, which my colleague was talking
about before, to ask questions about it.
So if I'm going to say, "Hey, what do you know about my work?"
it's probably going to give me a response back:
"This is what I know.
You like to work on machine learning projects.
Your main stack is this and this and this."
So it actually knows what I'm all about.
And if I can ask it, "Hey, what activities do I enjoy?"
it's going to give a reason back as well.
And you see on the left-hand side, it doesn't have a clue.
This AI system doesn't know.
But on the right-hand side, because we have
that long-term memory in place, it actually knows about me.
What we have also done in this specific scenario is we set
TTLs, times to live,
on the specific short-term and long-term memory.
So the short-term memory is only kept for 30 days.
And every single conversation I have
with this specific AI system is going to be saved for 30 days,
so I can jump to another one, or I can jump to,
"I also like sim racing," and stuff like that.
Now, the long-term, we're going to save
that a little bit longer, over a year, because I can be a user
and I can go away for two months, but the moment I'm going
to come back and interacting with the system,
I want this system to know about me.
So basically, how does this work?
And I'm going to jump to how it all works.
So basically, you send a message, "What are my hobbies?"
This generates a query embedding,
